adversary_notes: Two direct contradictions and one shared document. (1) MMED-h1#1 versus MMED-h2#5, same dockets, opposite conclusions. h2#5 is right. Both correctly find no S-4, Schedule TO or 425 for either CIK -- I re-ran both submission feeds and confirm it. But h1#1 then treats the 2026-09-01 lock-up lapse as making the split-off 'launchable from this print forward', which does not follow: Medtronic holds ~90% and has said since the IPO that it intends a generally tax-free distribution structured as spin-off, split-off or a combination, so a cash sale is off the table on tax grounds rather than on lock-up grounds, and carve-out lock-ups conventionally except transfers made in connection with the separation, meaning the lock-up was never the binding constraint. Decisively, Medtronic's own 2026-06-03 release guides FY27 EPS assuming twelve months of Diabetes consolidation and says the structure decision is not final -- that is a company telling you an exchange offer is not days away. A lock-up expiry is a supply event when the unlocked holder wants cash; this one does not and cannot take cash without breaking 355. It is also published: MarketBeat's lock-up calendar carries MMED at 9/2/2026. (2) MMED-h1#3 and MMED-h2#0 rest on the same document, Exhibit 99.1 of 2026-06-03, and that document defeats both of them in one sentence: FY27 organic growth of approximately 10% 'includes a 1.0 to 1.5% expected benefit from the extra week in FY27'. The extra week is inside the guidance, not concealed behind it, and Medtronic's release says its own FY27 guidance 'incorporates the 53rd week impact'. The harder question I was asked -- is it in consensus even though it is absent from wire copy -- resolves cleanly by arithmetic: the prior-year comparable quarter was $721m (Medtronic, 2025-08-19) and the pre-print consensus is $828.43m, which is +14.9%. You cannot get to +14.9% with flat FX and 8.7% underlying without the extra week. The street has it. h1#3's premise that the market anchors on 10% for this quarter is therefore wrong, and h2#0's 'roughly double the 8.7%' overstates what is really ~1.6x. Note also that the two findings point in opposite directions off the identical fact -- h1#3 reads it as an upside surprise to a 10% anchor, h2#0 as a warning that the headline is fake -- and both are wrong for the same reason. (3) On the short-interest claim, the specific hook fails on inspection: StockAnalysis.com prints 'Short % of Float 21.09%' and Finviz prints 'Short Float 22.59%' today, so the correct figure is on two of the most-used screens in the world; MarketBeat, the hunter's own source, is the one that divides by outstanding. The arithmetic is right and the position is real, but I think the read on it is wrong too -- in a pending parent/sub split-off the textbook trade is long parent, short sub, which means a meaningful slice of that 5.9m is stub arbitrage that will not chase a print in either direction. (4) On the baseline's 'downside paid' lean: with 833 contracts of total open interest and an ATM spread at 174% of mid, I would not give the +22.12 skew or the 4.59 put/call ratio any directional weight at all. That cuts both ways here -- no hunter on either side can claim the tape agrees with them, and no bullish finding can claim it is fighting a positioned market. The single 15.93% prior reaction is likewise one observation and a poor expected-move anchor for a name that has traded back to its $20 IPO price. Overall: this brief is unusually well sourced and unusually thoroughly pre-published. The most genuinely unpriced items are small and obscure -- the Italian Council of State referral in h2#2, and the in-quarter US demand-deferral inference in h2#3 -- and neither is worth more than about a point.
